gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus, one of the two units it showed, works as a UPS only through its three leftmost NEMA 5-20R outlets, which have a 1,440 W bypass limit and a 20 ms switching time, or that its 240 V output cannot be used while the unit is charging from a 120 V wall outlet. So a plug-in-and-forget setup covers 120 V loads such as a fridge, Wi-Fi and lights, but not a 240 V well pump or a 240 V transfer-switch feed.
standout_why: I read all five cited pages that I could open and compared them against this. itechguides sizing guide: it covers compressor surge and quotes only a DELTA Pro Ultra '0-ms' listing line. itechguides buying guide: it gives a general 120/240 V split-phase line and a '10ms UPS' listing blurb. outagereadyhq: it gives Jackery Smart Transfer Switch '20 ms' and covers which Anker switch fits one or two F3800 Plus units. ankersolix blog: it gives E10 '20 milliseconds'. calcpanel: it has no switchover or voltage material. None of them says which F3800 Plus outlets are UPS-protected, gives the 1,440 W bypass limit, or says 240 V is unavailable while the unit charges from 120 V. On neutral-ground bonding, none of the cited pages mentions it. The uncited watt48 (rank 7) says only that the unit's bonded neutral 'decides which kind of transfer equipment fits' and gives no status for any model. The cited PG&E PDF was not opened, so whether it mentions bonding is unchecked.
decides: This splits the shopper's two likely plans. (1) Leave the station plugged into the wall as an automatic UPS for the fridge and router: the F3800 Plus works if those loads stay on the three leftmost 5-20R outlets and under 1,440 W. (2) Use it for 240 V loads (well pump, transfer switch L14-30 feed) during an outage: that happens only on battery, after it is unplugged from 120 V charging, so it is not seamless. Before buying for a transfer switch, the shopper should check the station's neutral-ground bond against the switch. EcoFlow itself says an accidental neutral-ground connection can trip a GFCI. The finding confirms the F3800 Plus for 120 V essentials-UPS use and weakens it as a seamless 240 V backup. I could not get equivalent maker figures for the DELTA Pro 3 or Explorer 5000 Plus, so it does not yet rank them.

findings.label: UPS-protected outlets and bypass limit on wall power
findings.value: 3 leftmost NEMA 5-20R outlets; 1,440 W bypass limit
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus Portable Power Station (Anker SOLIX US product page, FAQ Q5)
findings.note: FAQ Q5, Condition 4 (no generator; plugged into a 120 V wall outlet): 'NEMA 5-20R (3 Leftmost Ports, UPS): Output available with bypass limit of up to 1,440W.'

findings.label: UPS switching time on wall power
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus Portable Power Station (Anker SOLIX US product page, FAQ Q5)
findings.note: FAQ Q5, Condition 4: 'Switching Time: 20 ms'. The page lists 30 ms and 50 ms only for generator transitions.

findings.label: 240 V output while charging from 120 V AC
findings.value: Not available (240 V output blocked while charging from 120 V AC)
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus Portable Power Station (Anker SOLIX US product page)
findings.note: Verbatim: '(Note: The 240V output cannot be used while the device is charging via 120V AC.)'

findings.label: 240 V transfer-switch port
findings.value: NEMA L14-30R, 120/240 V, 25 A max, 6,000 W max
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus Portable Power Station (Anker SOLIX US product page)
findings.note: Spec line: 'AC Output (NEMA L14-30R): 120V/240V~ 25A Max, 60Hz, 6000W Max'. FAQ Q4: 'Use the F3800 Plus's L14-30R AC output port to deliver up to 6,000W (240V)' to a transfer switch or inlet box.

findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus Portable Power Station (Anker SOLIX US product page)

findings.label: Neutral-ground bond mismatch with transfer equipment
findings.value: Accidental neutral-ground connection can trip a GFCI; mismatched setup creates unwanted current paths
findings.source_title: Floating Neutral Generator: What It Means and Why It Matters (EcoFlow, 2026-09-24)
findings.note: Verbatim: 'If neutral and ground connect by accident, the GFCI might trip, even if the generator is working well.' Also: 'Using a mismatched setup with the transfer equipment can create unwanted current paths' and 'Some equipment switches the neutral, but other systems keep it connected.' The page gives no bonding status for any specific EcoFlow station.
